q: In the Government system of classification of accounts, the capital outlay on village and small industries is accounted for under Major Head:

options.A: 4852 - Capital Outlay on Industries
options.B: 4853 - Capital Outlay on Non-ferrous Mining and Metallurgical Industries
options.C: 4885 - Capital Outlay on Other Outlays on Industries and Minerals
options.D: 4851 - Capital Outlay on Village and Small Industries

e: Under the List of Major and Minor Heads, 4851 is Capital Outlay on Village and Small Industries; 4852, 4853 and 4885 cover other industry groups, so village and small industries fall only under 4851.

q: Under the Finance Commission (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1951, one of the members of the Finance Commission is to be a person who:

options.A: Has special knowledge of economics
options.B: Is a serving officer of the Indian Audit and Accounts Service
options.C: Is a Member of Parliament nominated by the Speaker
options.D: Has been the Governor of the Reserve Bank of India

e: The Finance Commission (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1951 lays down member qualifications, one being a person having special knowledge of economics, along with judicial, finance and accounts, and administration experience.

q: Under Article 118 of the Constitution, the rules for regulating the procedure and the conduct of business of a House of Parliament are made by:

options.A: The President of India
options.B: That House itself, subject to the provisions of the Constitution
options.C: The Public Accounts Committee
options.D: The Comptroller and Auditor General of India

e: Article 118 provides that each House of Parliament may make rules for regulating, subject to the Constitution, its procedure and conduct of business, so the rule-making power lies with that House itself.

q: Under Article 122 of the Constitution, the validity of any proceedings in Parliament:

options.A: Can be set aside by the Supreme Court on any ground whatsoever
options.B: Is decided finally by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India
options.C: Shall not be called in question on the ground of any alleged irregularity of procedure
options.D: Can be questioned only by the Public Accounts Committee

e: Article 122(1) bars questioning the validity of any proceedings in Parliament on the ground of any alleged irregularity of procedure, protecting internal proceedings from outside challenge on that ground.

q: An 'audit programme' drawn up for the audit of a unit primarily sets out:

options.A: The sanctions accorded for the expenditure of the unit during the year
options.B: The replies furnished by the unit to earlier audit objections
options.C: The budget allotments placed at the disposal of the unit
options.D: The audit work to be done, its scope and extent, and the distribution of that work among the members of the audit party

e: An audit programme sets out in advance the audit work to be done, its scope and extent, and how that work is distributed among audit party members, guiding orderly and complete coverage.

q: 'Professional scepticism' in audit requires the auditor to:

options.A: Maintain a questioning mind and a critical assessment of the audit evidence, without assuming either dishonesty or unqualified honesty on the part of the management
options.B: Assume that the accounts of the audited unit are fraudulent until the contrary is proved
options.C: Accept all explanations offered by the management without corroboration
options.D: Restrict the audit to the arithmetical checking of the accounts only

e: Professional scepticism under auditing standards means a questioning mind and critical assessment of evidence, neither assuming dishonesty nor unqualified honesty, but corroborating management assertions.

q: A 'forensic audit' is best described as an audit:

options.A: Conducted only of the forensic science laboratories of the Government
options.B: Directed specifically to the detection and investigation of fraud, the findings of which are capable of being used in legal proceedings
options.C: Conducted after the close of the financial year with reference to the Appropriation Accounts
options.D: Conducted by the internal audit wing as a matter of routine every year

e: Forensic audit is directed to detection and investigation of fraud, conducted so that findings are capable of being used as evidence in legal proceedings, unlike a routine financial audit.

q: 'Teeming and lading', a technique of defalcation in cash accounts, consists of:

options.A: Preparing two sets of accounts for one and the same transaction
options.B: Charging personal expenditure to the office accounts of the Government
options.C: Misappropriating a receipt from one party and covering it up by appropriating a later receipt from another party towards it, and so on in succession
options.D: Showing receipts in the accounts at figures higher than those actually received

e: Teeming and lading is defalcation where a receipt from one party is misappropriated and a later receipt from another party is credited to the first, the shortage being rolled forward in succession.

q: 'Window dressing' of accounts means:

options.A: Presenting the accounts in a neat and legible form for inspection by Audit
options.B: Appending full explanations for variations in the Appropriation Accounts
options.C: Reconciling the subsidiary registers with the general books at regular intervals
options.D: Manipulating the accounts, by recording or omitting transactions, so as to present a financial position more favourable than the real one

e: Window dressing means manipulating accounts by recording or omitting transactions to present a financial position more favourable than the real one, rather than merely presenting accounts neatly.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes grants-in-aid under Article 275 of the Constitution from grants under Article 282?

options.A: Grants under Article 275 are statutory grants, charged on the Consolidated Fund of India and made on the principles recommended by the Finance Commission, while grants under Article 282 are discretionary grants which the Union may make for any public purpose
options.B: Grants under Article 275 are discretionary, while grants under Article 282 are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India
options.C: Grants under both the Articles are made only on the recommendation of the Finance Commission
options.D: There is no difference between the two, both being voted grants made for any public purpose

e: Article 275 grants are statutory, charged on the Consolidated Fund of India and based on Finance Commission principles, while Article 282 grants are discretionary and may be made for any public purpose.

q: A 'Pigouvian subsidy' is a subsidy granted by the Government in order to:

options.A: Compensate the States for the loss of revenue on the introduction of a new tax
options.B: Encourage an activity which generates a positive externality, so that the level of that activity is raised towards the socially optimum level
options.C: Meet the revenue deficit of a public sector undertaking
options.D: Finance the repayment of the public debt of the Government

e: A Pigouvian subsidy encourages an activity generating a positive externality, raising its level towards the socially optimum level where private activity alone would be below that optimum.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. A sinking fund for the redemption of public debt is built up by periodic appropriations, so that a sum sufficient to redeem the debt is accumulated by the date on which the debt falls due for repayment.
2. The Consolidated Sinking Fund set up by the State Governments for the amortisation of their borrowings is maintained in the Public Account of the State.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: A sinking fund accumulates periodic appropriations to redeem debt at maturity, and the Consolidated Sinking Fund of States for amortising borrowings is maintained in the Public Account, so both statements hold.

q: ASOSAI, the regional organisation of Supreme Audit Institutions of which the Comptroller and Auditor General of India is a member, stands for:

options.A: Association of South Asian Audit Institutions
options.B: Asian Society of Auditors International
options.C: Asian Organization of Supreme Audit Institutions
options.D: Association of Supreme Audit Institutions of Asia-Pacific

e: ASOSAI stands for Asian Organization of Supreme Audit Institutions, the INTOSAI regional group of Asian supreme audit institutions, of which the CAG of India is a member.

q: The 'Receipts Budget' document presented to Parliament along with the Annual Financial Statement primarily contains:

options.A: The detailed Demands for Grants of each Ministry and Department
options.B: The explanations for variations between the actual expenditure and the final grant
options.C: The certificate of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on the Finance Accounts
options.D: An analysis of the tax and non-tax revenue receipts and the capital receipts of the Government, with the details of the sources from which they are expected to be realised

e: The Receipts Budget analyses tax and non-tax revenue receipts and capital receipts of Government, detailing the sources from which receipts are expected, unlike Demands for Grants or Finance Accounts.

q: Two taxpayers, whose incomes and family circumstances are identical in all material respects, are assessed to tax at very different burdens without any justification based on a difference in their circumstances. The tax system, in this respect, offends against the principle of:

options.A: Vertical equity
options.B: The benefit principle of taxation
options.C: The ability-to-pay principle, as distinct from equity between equals
options.D: Horizontal equity

e: Horizontal equity requires equals to be treated equally; identical taxpayers bearing very different burdens without justification offends horizontal, not vertical, equity which concerns unequals.

q: In audit, 'vouching' primarily means:

options.A: Checking the entries in the books of account against the supporting documentary evidence, so as to establish their authenticity
options.B: Physically verifying the assets shown in the balance sheet on the closing date
options.C: Checking only the arithmetical accuracy of the totals in the books of account
options.D: Comparing the accounts of the current year with those of the previous year

e: Vouching is checking entries in the books against supporting documentary evidence to establish authenticity, accuracy and authorisation of the transactions recorded.

q: 'Routine checking' in audit consists mainly of:

options.A: Examining the system of internal control operating in the audited unit
options.B: Obtaining written confirmations of balances from outside parties
options.C: Checking casts and sub-casts, postings from one book to another, and the arithmetical accuracy of the books of account
options.D: Evaluating whether a programme has achieved its intended objectives

e: Routine checking covers checking casts and sub-casts, postings from one book to another, and arithmetical accuracy of accounts, forming the basic mechanical check in audit.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes 'verification' of assets from 'vouching' in audit?

options.A: Verification is confined to the arithmetical accuracy of the ledger, while vouching relates to the physical existence of assets
options.B: Verification and vouching are two names for one and the same audit procedure
options.C: Verification is carried out only by the executive staff, while vouching is carried out only by the auditor
options.D: Verification seeks to establish the existence, ownership and title of assets as on the date of the balance sheet, while vouching tests entries in the books against documentary evidence

e: Verification establishes existence, ownership and title of assets on the balance sheet date, while vouching tests book entries against documentary evidence; the two procedures are distinct.

q: In audit, 'valuation' of assets and liabilities refers to ascertaining that:

options.A: The assets physically exist in the custody of the audited unit
options.B: The assets and liabilities are shown in the balance sheet at their proper values
options.C: Every entry in the books is supported by a voucher
options.D: The assets are legally owned by the audited unit

e: Valuation in audit means ascertaining that assets and liabilities are shown in the balance sheet at proper values, distinct from physical existence, ownership or vouching of entries.

q: 'External confirmation' as a source of audit evidence means:

options.A: A certificate obtained from the head of the audited office
options.B: A comparison of the audited figures with the budget estimates
options.C: Audit evidence obtained by the auditor as a direct written response from a third party outside the audited entity
options.D: A report obtained from the internal audit wing of the organisation

e: External confirmation is audit evidence obtained by the auditor as a direct written response from a third party outside the audited entity, for example on balances due.

q: A 'negative confirmation' request in audit asks the third party to respond:

options.A: Only if the third party disagrees with the information stated in the request
options.B: In all cases, whether the stated information is correct or not
options.C: Only through the audited entity and not directly to the auditor
options.D: Only after the audit report has been issued

e: A negative confirmation request asks the third party to respond only if it disagrees with the information stated, silence being taken as agreement with the stated balance.

q: An auditor writes to a debtor requesting him to confirm the balance shown as due from him, and to reply in every case, whether he agrees with the balance or not. This is an instance of:

options.A: Negative confirmation
options.B: A management representation
options.C: An analytical procedure
options.D: Positive confirmation

e: Asking a debtor to confirm the balance and to reply in every case, whether he agrees or not, is positive confirmation, because a response is required in all cases.

q: Audit evidence obtained by an auditor is, in its general character:

options.A: Always conclusive proof of the matter to which it relates
options.B: Of no value unless it is documentary in form
options.C: Persuasive rather than conclusive, so that the auditor forms conclusions by evaluating evidence from different sources together
options.D: Acceptable only when it is obtained from outside the audited entity

e: Audit evidence is persuasive rather than conclusive; the auditor evaluates evidence from different sources together to form conclusions, and documentary form alone does not decide its value.

q: 'Sampling risk' in audit arises because:

options.A: The auditor may fail to detect a fraud committed by the management
options.B: The records of the audited unit are incomplete
options.C: The conclusion reached by the auditor on the basis of a sample may differ from the conclusion that would have been reached if the whole population had been examined
options.D: The sample selected is larger than is necessary for the audit

e: Sampling risk is the risk that the conclusion based on a sample may differ from the conclusion that would have been reached if the whole population had been examined in the same way.

q: Under 'stratified sampling' in audit:

options.A: The population is divided into sub-populations or strata, such as high-value and low-value items, and a sample is drawn from each stratum
options.B: Every item in the population is examined in full
options.C: Items are selected purely at the personal convenience of the auditor
options.D: Items are selected at a fixed interval through the population after a random start

e: Stratified sampling divides the population into sub-populations or strata, such as high-value and low-value items, and draws a sample from each stratum to improve representativeness.

q: Selection of sample items in audit at a constant interval, after choosing the starting point at random, is known as:

options.A: Stratified selection
options.B: Block selection
options.C: Haphazard selection
options.D: Systematic selection

e: Systematic selection chooses sample items at a constant interval through the population after a random start, unlike stratified, block or haphazard selection methods.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes a 'permanent audit file' from a 'current audit file'?

options.A: The permanent audit file is maintained by the audited entity, while the current audit file is maintained by the auditor
options.B: The permanent audit file contains matter of continuing importance to the audit, such as the rules, organisational set-up and long-term arrangements of the unit, while the current audit file contains the working papers relating to the particular period under audit
options.C: The permanent audit file contains only correspondence, while the current audit file contains only vouchers
options.D: There is no distinction between the two files

e: The permanent audit file holds matter of continuing importance such as rules, organisation and long-term arrangements, while the current file holds working papers for the particular period audited.

q: The working papers prepared by an auditor in the course of an audit are, as a general rule, the property of:

options.A: The audited entity, which may call for them at any time
options.B: The Public Accounts Committee
options.C: The auditor (audit office), who retains them to support the conclusions reached in the audit
options.D: The Ministry of Finance

e: Audit working papers are, as a general rule, the property of the auditor or audit office, retained to support conclusions reached and to evidence work performed in the audit.

q: A 'management letter' issued by an auditor primarily serves to:

options.A: Bring to the notice of the management the weaknesses in internal control and related matters noticed during the audit, for remedial action
options.B: Convey the auditor's final opinion on the accounts to Parliament
options.C: Authorise the management to incur expenditure in excess of the grant
options.D: Settle the audit objections raised in the inspection report

e: A management letter brings weaknesses in internal control and related matters noticed during audit to management notice for remedial action; it is not the audit opinion to Parliament.

q: An 'audit trail' in an accounting system means:

options.A: The programme showing the dates on which different units will be audited
options.B: The list of audit objections outstanding against a unit
options.C: The route followed by an audit party while touring field units
options.D: A chronological record by which a transaction can be traced from its source document through the books of account to the final statements, and vice versa

e: An audit trail is the chronological record by which a transaction can be traced from its source document through the books to the final statements, and vice versa.

q: Pro forma accounts are prepared for a departmental commercial undertaking of the Government primarily in order to:

options.A: Replace the regular Government accounts maintained for the undertaking
options.B: Bring out the commercial or working result of the undertaking, as if it were run on commercial lines
options.C: Enable the undertaking to escape audit by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India
options.D: Show the grant-wise position of its expenditure for the Appropriation Accounts

e: Pro forma accounts are prepared for a departmental commercial undertaking to bring out its commercial or working result as if run on commercial lines, supplementing cash-based Government accounts.

q: The adjustments which are peculiar to pro forma accounts, and which do not find a place in the regular Government accounts of a departmental undertaking, include adjustments on account of:

options.A: Cash receipts and cash payments of the undertaking
options.B: Salaries of the staff borne in the regular accounts
options.C: Grants received from the Consolidated Fund of India
options.D: Interest on the Government capital invested in the undertaking and depreciation of its assets

e: Adjustments peculiar to pro forma accounts include interest on Government capital invested and depreciation of assets, which have no cash outgo and do not appear in regular Government accounts.

q: Which of the following correctly describes the position of pro forma accounts in relation to the regular Government accounts?

options.A: The regular Government accounts of the undertaking continue to be maintained in the usual form, and the pro forma accounts are supplementary accounts prepared in addition to them
options.B: Once pro forma accounts are introduced, the regular Government accounts of the undertaking are discontinued
options.C: Pro forma accounts are a part of the Finance Accounts of the Union Government
options.D: Pro forma accounts are prepared only when the undertaking earns a profit

e: Regular Government accounts of the undertaking continue in the usual form; pro forma accounts are supplementary accounts prepared in addition to them, not a replacement for them.

q: The final accounts drawn up under the pro forma system for a departmental commercial undertaking generally comprise:

options.A: Only a statement of stores issued during the year
options.B: Only the Appropriation Accounts of the undertaking
options.C: A Manufacturing or Trading Account, a Profit and Loss Account and a Balance Sheet
options.D: Only a cash book and a general ledger

e: Final pro forma accounts of a departmental commercial undertaking generally comprise a Manufacturing or Trading Account, a Profit and Loss Account and a Balance Sheet on commercial lines.

q: A 'continuous audit' is an audit in which:

options.A: Every transaction of the unit is checked in full, dispensing with test checks altogether
options.B: The audit is carried out only after the close of the financial year
options.C: The auditor's staff attends at regular intervals during the year itself and examines the accounts up to the date of each visit
options.D: The audit is conducted without any break until the accounts of the whole organisation are certified

e: In continuous audit the auditor staff attends at regular intervals during the year itself and examines accounts up to the date of each visit, instead of waiting until after year-end.

q: A 'partial audit' is an audit which:

options.A: Is conducted by an auditor who is not fully qualified
options.B: Is confined to a part only of the accounts, or to a specific aspect or period, instead of extending to the whole of the accounts
options.C: Is conducted on the basis of a sample of transactions
options.D: Remains incomplete because the audited unit fails to produce the records called for

e: Partial audit is confined to only a part of the accounts, or to a specific aspect or period, instead of extending to the whole accounts, and does not mean an unqualified or sample audit.

q: An Internal Control Questionnaire is used in audit primarily to:

options.A: Record the replies given by the audited unit to individual audit objections
options.B: Fix the fees payable to the auditor
options.C: List the vouchers to be checked during local audit
options.D: Obtain and evaluate, through a structured set of questions, information about the system of internal control operating in the unit

e: An Internal Control Questionnaire obtains and evaluates, through a structured set of questions, information about the system of internal control operating in the audited unit.

q: In an office, the same official places orders for stores, receives and inspects the stores, and also authorises payment of the bills for them. The principal weakness in internal control disclosed by this arrangement is the absence of:

options.A: Segregation of duties, under which the functions of authorisation, custody and recording of a transaction are divided among different officials
options.B: A system of budgetary control over stores expenditure
options.C: Periodical stock verification by stock verifiers
options.D: Pre-check of bills by the Accounts office

e: One official ordering, receiving and inspecting stores and authorising payment violates segregation of duties, which divides authorisation, custody and recording among different officials to prevent fraud and error.

q: A 'surprise check' by audit or by a supervisory authority is characterised by the fact that it is carried out:

options.A: Only at the close of the financial year
options.B: Without prior intimation to the custodian of the cash, stores or records to be checked
options.C: Only in units where a fraud has already been detected
options.D: Only with the prior approval of the Public Accounts Committee

e: A surprise check is carried out without prior intimation to the custodian of cash, stores or records, so the actual position is found as it normally exists.

q: 'Cut-off' procedures in audit are directed to ensuring that:

options.A: The audit of a unit is completed within the time allotted in the audit programme
options.B: Outstanding audit objections are dropped after a prescribed period
options.C: Transactions occurring near the end of an accounting period are recorded in the accounts of the correct period
options.D: The sample selected for test check is cut down to a manageable size

e: Cut-off procedures ensure transactions near the end of an accounting period are recorded in the correct period, preventing shifting of receipts or expenditure between periods.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Written representations obtained from the management form part of the audit evidence available to the auditor.
2. Written representations from the management can be accepted as a substitute for other audit evidence which the auditor could reasonably expect to obtain.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Management written representations are audit evidence, but under auditing standards they are not a substitute for other evidence the auditor could reasonably expect to obtain, so only statement 1 is correct.

q: In the framework of internal control, the 'control environment' of an organisation refers to:

options.A: The physical safeguards provided for the protection of cash and stores
options.B: The computer system in which the accounts of the organisation are maintained
options.C: The external audit arrangements applicable to the organisation
options.D: The overall foundation of internal control, comprising the integrity and ethical values, management philosophy, organisational structure and assignment of authority and responsibility in the organisation

e: Control environment is the foundation of internal control, comprising integrity and ethical values, management philosophy, organisational structure and assignment of authority and responsibility.

q: Flow charts are used by auditors as a method of:

options.A: Presenting the findings of a performance audit to Parliament
options.B: Recording and depicting, in diagrammatic form, the flow of documents and procedures in a system, for the study and evaluation of internal control
options.C: Computing the sample size for a test check
options.D: Showing the trend of expenditure of a unit over a number of years

e: Flow charts record and depict in diagrammatic form the flow of documents and procedures in a system, helping the auditor study and evaluate internal control.

q: A 'balance sheet audit' is best described as an audit approach in which:

options.A: Only the cash balance of the unit is verified
options.B: The audit is confined to checking the arithmetical accuracy of the balance sheet
options.C: The verification starts from the balance sheet or final accounts and the items appearing therein are traced and verified with the supporting records and evidence
options.D: The balance sheet is audited by the executive instead of by the statutory auditor

e: Balance sheet audit starts from the balance sheet or final accounts and traces and verifies items appearing therein with supporting records and evidence.

q: Under Article 146 of the Constitution, the administrative expenses of the office of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India, including salaries, allowances and pensions payable to persons serving in that office:

options.A: Are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India
options.B: Are voted annually by Parliament as a part of the Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Finance
options.C: Are met out of the Public Account of India
options.D: Are borne by the State Governments in proportion to the audit work done for them

e: Article 146 provides that administrative expenses of the CAG office, including salaries, allowances and pensions of persons serving in that office, are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.

q: Under Article 146 of the Constitution, the conditions of service of the persons serving in the Indian Audit and Accounts Department are determined by:

options.A: The Comptroller and Auditor General of India by his own orders
options.B: Parliament by resolution of both Houses
options.C: The Public Accounts Committee
options.D: Rules made by the President after consultation with the Comptroller and Auditor General of India

e: Article 146 provides that conditions of service of persons serving in the Indian Audit and Accounts Department are prescribed by rules made by the President after consultation with the CAG.

q: The hypothesis of 'Ricardian equivalence' in public finance holds that:

options.A: An increase in Government expenditure is always matched by an equal increase in revenue
options.B: Financing Government expenditure by borrowing, instead of by taxation, does not stimulate aggregate demand, because taxpayers save more in anticipation of the higher future taxes needed to service the debt
options.C: Public debt is never a burden on future generations
options.D: Taxation and borrowing have identical effects on the distribution of income

e: Ricardian equivalence holds that debt financing instead of taxation does not stimulate demand because taxpayers save more in anticipation of higher future taxes needed to service the debt.

q: The 'absolute taxable capacity' of a community refers to:

options.A: The proportion in which the tax burden is shared between two communities
options.B: The maximum revenue which the taxation of the community can yield in a year at the prevailing rates
options.C: The upper limit of taxation, in absolute money terms, beyond which taxation begins to produce harmful effects on production, enterprise and the economy
options.D: The taxable capacity of the community measured only by its income-tax collections

e: Absolute taxable capacity is the upper limit of taxation of a community in absolute money terms, beyond which taxation harms production, enterprise and the economy.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes 'relative taxable capacity' from 'absolute taxable capacity'?

options.A: Relative taxable capacity compares the taxable capacity of two or more communities or groups in relation to each other, while absolute taxable capacity concerns the limit of taxation of a single community considered by itself
options.B: Relative taxable capacity is measured in money terms, while absolute taxable capacity cannot be measured at all
options.C: Relative taxable capacity applies only to direct taxes, while absolute taxable capacity applies only to indirect taxes
options.D: There is no distinction between the two concepts

e: Relative taxable capacity compares taxable capacity of two or more communities in relation to each other, while absolute taxable capacity concerns the limit for a single community by itself.

q: 'Automatic stabilisers' (built-in stabilisers) in the fiscal system are mechanisms which:

options.A: Require a fresh decision of the Government on each occasion before they can operate
options.B: Operate only in the monetary policy of the central bank
options.C: Are built into the tax and expenditure structure, such as progressive income taxation and unemployment relief, and dampen economic fluctuations without fresh discretionary action
options.D: Stabilise the prices of essential commodities through buffer stock operations

e: Automatic stabilisers are built into the tax and expenditure structure, such as progressive income tax and unemployment relief, and dampen fluctuations without fresh discretionary decisions.

q: During a recession, the tax revenues of the Government fall and its expenditure on relief and social security rises automatically, widening the budget deficit without any new policy decision. This illustrates the working of:

options.A: The displacement effect in public expenditure
options.B: Built-in (automatic) stabilisers in the fiscal system
options.C: Tax capitalisation
options.D: The crowding-out effect of public borrowing

e: Falling tax revenue and rising relief and social security spending in a recession, widening the deficit without new policy, illustrate built-in automatic stabilisers working through the fiscal system.

q: The 'structural deficit' of a Government is that part of its fiscal deficit which:

options.A: Would persist even if the economy were operating at its full-employment or potential level of output
options.B: Arises solely on account of a depression in the economy
options.C: Relates only to expenditure on capital works
options.D: Is caused by the issue of Treasury Bills during the year

e: Structural deficit is the part of fiscal deficit that would persist even if the economy operated at full-employment or potential output, unlike the cyclical part caused by a downturn.

q: 'Fiscal transparency' in the management of public finances primarily requires that:

options.A: All Government expenditure is kept outside the budget documents
options.B: Tax rates are not disclosed to the taxpayers in advance
options.C: The fiscal position, policies and accounts of the Government are presented clearly, completely and openly, so that the true state of public finances can be assessed
options.D: The budget is presented to Parliament in a closed session

e: Fiscal transparency requires the fiscal position, policies and accounts of Government to be presented clearly, completely and openly so the true state of public finances can be assessed.

q: Borrowings described as 'off-budget borrowings' are borrowings which:

options.A: Are raised by the Government after the budget has been presented
options.B: Form a part of the internal debt shown in the Finance Accounts
options.C: Are raised in foreign currency only
options.D: Are raised by public sector entities or agencies on the direction of the Government, and are serviced out of the Government budget, but do not appear directly as borrowings of the Government itself in its fiscal deficit

e: Off-budget borrowings are raised by public sector entities on Government direction and serviced from the budget, but do not appear directly as Government borrowings in its fiscal deficit.

q: A 'sunset clause' attached to a tax incentive or exemption provides that:

options.A: The incentive will continue indefinitely until it is expressly repealed
options.B: The incentive will cease to have effect after a specified date, unless it is renewed
options.C: The incentive applies only to taxes levied by the State Governments
options.D: The proceeds of the tax will be shared with the States after a specified date

e: A sunset clause provides that a tax incentive or exemption will cease to have effect after a specified date unless it is renewed, preventing indefinite continuation.

q: The principle of inter-generational equity in public borrowing implies that:

options.A: The burden of a public loan should, as far as possible, fall on the generations which derive benefit from the expenditure financed by it, rather than being shifted unfairly to future generations which derive no such benefit
options.B: All public loans should be repaid within the year in which they are raised
options.C: Future generations should bear the entire burden of the present Government's expenditure
options.D: Public borrowing should be resorted to only for meeting revenue expenditure

e: Inter-generational equity in borrowing requires the burden of a public loan to fall, as far as possible, on generations deriving benefit from the expenditure it finances.

q: The public debt of a Government is regarded as sustainable when:

options.A: The Government borrows afresh every year to repay all its maturing loans
options.B: The Government can continue to service its debt, and the debt does not grow without limit in relation to the income of the economy, without requiring default or an abrupt fiscal correction
options.C: The debt of the Government is owed entirely to its own central bank
options.D: The Government maintains a revenue surplus in every year without exception

e: Public debt is sustainable when Government can continue servicing it and debt does not grow without limit in relation to national income, without default or abrupt fiscal correction.

q: A Government which raises its expenditure and reduces taxes during a recession, and restrains expenditure and raises revenues during a boom, is following:

options.A: A policy of functional finance only
options.B: A balanced-budget policy for every year
options.C: A pro-cyclical fiscal policy
options.D: A counter-cyclical fiscal policy

e: Raising expenditure and cutting taxes in recession and restraining expenditure and raising revenue in a boom is counter-cyclical fiscal policy, opposite to a pro-cyclical policy.

q: The gross traffic earnings of a zonal railway increase during a year, while its working expenses remain unchanged. Other things being equal, the Operating Ratio of the railway will:

options.A: Increase, showing a deterioration in its working
options.B: Decrease, showing an improvement in its working
options.C: Remain unchanged, as it is not affected by earnings
options.D: Become equal to its return on capital-at-charge

e: Operating Ratio is working expenses as a percentage of gross traffic earnings; if earnings rise and expenses are unchanged, the ratio falls, showing improved working.

q: The primary responsibility for establishing and maintaining a sound system of internal control in a Government office rests with:

options.A: The Comptroller and Auditor General of India
options.B: The head of the office and the management of the organisation concerned
options.C: The Public Accounts Committee
options.D: The internal audit party posted in the office

e: Primary responsibility for establishing and maintaining a sound internal control system rests with the head of office and management of the organisation, not with external audit or the PAC.

q: Under Article 248 of the Constitution, the residuary power of legislation, in respect of any matter not enumerated in the Concurrent List or the State List, vests exclusively in:

options.A: Parliament
options.B: The State Legislatures
options.C: Parliament and the State Legislatures concurrently
options.D: The President, acting by Ordinance

e: Article 248 vests residuary power of legislation on matters not enumerated in the Concurrent List or State List exclusively in Parliament, including residuary taxation power.

q: An Ordinance promulgated by the President under Article 123 of the Constitution can be issued when:

options.A: Parliament is in session and a Bill on the subject is pending
options.B: Parliament is not in session and the President is satisfied that circumstances exist which render it necessary for him to take immediate action
options.C: The Supreme Court recommends immediate legislation
options.D: The Council of States alone is not in session

e: Article 123 empowers the President to promulgate an Ordinance only when Parliament is not in session and he is satisfied circumstances require immediate action; it then has force of law temporarily.

q: Integrated Goods and Services Tax (IGST) is the tax levied on:

options.A: Supplies of goods and services within a State only
options.B: Imports into a State from another State for resale only
options.C: Inter-State supplies of goods and services, levied and collected by the Centre
options.D: Supplies made by the Central Government to its own departments

e: IGST is levied and collected by the Centre on inter-State supplies of goods and services, including imports treated as inter-State supplies, unlike intra-State CGST and SGST.

q: The mechanism of Input Tax Credit under the Goods and Services Tax primarily enables a registered dealer to:

options.A: Claim a refund of the entire tax collected on his sales
options.B: Pay tax only on the profit margin of each transaction
options.C: Recover the tax paid on his inputs from the Government in cash
options.D: Set off the tax paid on inputs against the tax payable on his output supplies, so that tax is borne ultimately on the value added

e: Input Tax Credit allows a registered dealer to set off tax paid on inputs against tax payable on output supplies, so tax is ultimately borne on value added at each stage.

q: Under the 'reverse charge' mechanism in the Goods and Services Tax, the liability to pay the tax on a supply rests on:

options.A: The recipient of the goods or services, instead of the supplier
options.B: The transporter who carries the goods
options.C: The bank through which the payment is made
options.D: The Central Government, on behalf of the supplier

e: Under reverse charge in GST, liability to pay tax on a supply rests on the recipient of goods or services instead of the supplier, for notified categories and supplies.

q: In the Goods and Services Tax system, the 'place of supply' of a transaction is significant chiefly because it determines:

options.A: The rate of penalty for late payment of tax
options.B: Whether the supply is inter-State or intra-State, and accordingly whether IGST or CGST with SGST applies
options.C: The authority competent to register the dealer
options.D: The period within which the return must be filed

e: Place of supply determines whether a supply is inter-State or intra-State, and accordingly whether IGST or CGST with SGST applies to the transaction.

q: Computer-Assisted Audit Techniques (CAATs) in audit refer to:

options.A: The computerisation of the auditee's accounting system
options.B: The issue of audit reports in electronic form only
options.C: The use of computer software and tools by the auditor to extract, sort and analyse data from the auditee's systems for audit purposes
options.D: The replacement of audit sampling by manual checking

e: Computer-Assisted Audit Techniques are computer software and tools used by the auditor to extract, sort and analyse data from the auditee systems for audit purposes.

q: The principal advantage of applying data analytics in the audit of a large computerised accounting system is that it enables the auditor to:

options.A: Dispense with the evaluation of internal controls altogether
options.B: Certify the accounts without examining any individual transaction
options.C: Reduce the audit to a review of exception reports generated by the auditee
options.D: Examine the entire population of transactions and identify anomalies, patterns and unusual items for focused audit scrutiny

e: Data analytics in a large computerised system enables the auditor to examine the entire population of transactions and identify anomalies, patterns and unusual items for focused scrutiny.

q: In the 'Three Lines' model of governance and risk management, internal audit constitutes the:

options.A: Third line, providing independent assurance over governance, risk management and controls
options.B: First line, owning and managing risks in day-to-day operations
options.C: Second line, providing risk and compliance support to operations
options.D: External line, replacing the statutory audit

e: In the Three Lines model, internal audit is the third line, providing independent assurance over governance, risk management and controls, separate from operations and risk support lines.

q: An Audit Committee in a large organisation primarily strengthens internal audit by:

options.A: Carrying out the day-to-day audit fieldwork itself
options.B: Providing oversight of the internal audit function, safeguarding its independence and ensuring follow-up on its findings
options.C: Preparing the accounts which internal audit then examines
options.D: Fixing the pay and postings of the audit staff

e: An Audit Committee strengthens internal audit by providing oversight of the function, safeguarding its independence and ensuring follow-up on its findings, not by doing fieldwork itself.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Unusual transactions near the close of the accounting period and significant unexplained changes in ratios or balances are among the 'red flags' that alert an auditor to the possibility of fraud.
2. The presence of a red flag by itself establishes that a fraud has been committed.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Unusual period-end transactions and unexplained changes in ratios are red flags alerting the auditor to possible fraud, but a red flag alone does not establish fraud, so only statement 1 is correct.

q: Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) in Government expenditure refers to a system under which:

options.A: Subsidies are paid to manufacturers instead of to consumers
options.B: Grants are released to State Governments in a single instalment
options.C: Funds are transferred through a chain of intermediate agencies before reaching the beneficiary
options.D: Benefits and subsidies are transferred directly into the bank or postal accounts of the identified beneficiaries

e: Direct Benefit Transfer transfers benefits and subsidies directly into bank or postal accounts of identified beneficiaries, removing intermediate agencies and leakages.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes asset monetisation from strategic disinvestment?

options.A: Asset monetisation does not involve transfer of ownership or management control of the underlying public asset, whereas strategic disinvestment involves transfer of ownership and management control to a strategic partner
options.B: Asset monetisation applies only to land, whereas strategic disinvestment applies only to shares
options.C: In asset monetisation the asset is sold permanently, whereas in strategic disinvestment it is only leased out
options.D: There is no material difference between the two

e: Asset monetisation involves no transfer of ownership or management control of the public asset, while strategic disinvestment transfers ownership and management control to a strategic partner.

q: The Department of Investment and Public Asset Management (DIPAM) functions as a department of:

options.A: The Ministry of Corporate Affairs
options.B: The Ministry of Finance, dealing with investment in, and disinvestment and management of, the public assets of the Central Government
options.C: The Reserve Bank of India
options.D: NITI Aayog

e: DIPAM is a department of the Ministry of Finance dealing with investment in, and disinvestment and management of, public assets of the Central Government.

q: 'Open market operations' of the Reserve Bank of India consist of:

options.A: Direct lending by the Reserve Bank to State Governments
options.B: Sale of foreign currency in the exchange market
options.C: Outright purchase and sale of Government securities by the Reserve Bank for adjusting the liquidity in the banking system
options.D: Fixing of interest rates on small savings schemes

e: Open market operations are outright purchase and sale of Government securities by the Reserve Bank of India to adjust liquidity in the banking system.

q: In the Lok Sabha, 'Zero Hour' refers to the period:

options.A: Reserved for the discussion of the Budget
options.B: During which starred questions are answered orally
options.C: Set apart for the voting of Demands for Grants
options.D: Immediately following the Question Hour, during which members may raise matters without prior notice

e: Zero Hour in Lok Sabha is the period immediately following Question Hour during which members may raise matters without prior notice, an Indian parliamentary practice.

q: An adjournment motion in the Lok Sabha is moved primarily for the purpose of:

options.A: Discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, interrupting the normal business of the House
options.B: Expressing want of confidence in the Council of Ministers
options.C: Reducing the amount of a Demand for Grant
options.D: Seeking the removal of the Speaker

e: An adjournment motion is moved to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance, interrupting normal business of the House, and involves an element of censure.

q: A motion of no-confidence in the Council of Ministers can be moved only in:

options.A: The Rajya Sabha
options.B: The Lok Sabha
options.C: Either House of Parliament
options.D: A joint sitting of the two Houses

e: A motion of no-confidence in the Council of Ministers can be moved only in the Lok Sabha, because the Council is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha under Article 75.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes a censure motion from a motion of no-confidence?

options.A: A censure motion can be moved in either House, while a no-confidence motion can be moved only in the Rajya Sabha
options.B: A censure motion does not require any reason to be stated, while a no-confidence motion must state the reasons in full
options.C: A censure motion may be moved against an individual Minister or a group of Ministers and should state the reasons for it, while a no-confidence motion is moved against the Council of Ministers as a whole and need not state reasons
options.D: Adoption of a censure motion invariably requires the Council of Ministers to resign, while adoption of a no-confidence motion does not

e: A censure motion may target an individual Minister or group and must state reasons, while a no-confidence motion is against the Council of Ministers as a whole and need not state reasons.

q: In the Question Hour of Parliament, a 'starred' question is one which is:

options.A: Answered in writing and laid on the Table of the House
options.B: Asked by the Leader of the Opposition only
options.C: Marked for answer during the Zero Hour
options.D: Distinguished by an asterisk and answered orally in the House, with supplementaries permitted

e: A starred question is distinguished by an asterisk and answered orally in the House, with supplementaries permitted, unlike unstarred questions answered in written form.

q: Article 301 of the Constitution declares that, subject to the other provisions of that Part:

options.A: Trade, commerce and intercourse throughout the territory of India shall be free
options.B: No tax shall be levied on the movement of goods between States
options.C: Parliament alone may regulate all trade within a State
options.D: States may impose any restriction on trade in the public interest without restriction

e: Article 301 declares that, subject to other provisions of Part XIII, trade, commerce and intercourse throughout the territory of India shall be free.

q: The Punchhi Commission, whose report dealt with the working of the existing arrangements between the Union and the States, was a commission on:

options.A: Electoral reforms
options.B: Centre-State relations
options.C: Judicial reforms
options.D: Police reforms

e: The Punchhi Commission was the Commission on Centre-State Relations, set up to examine working of existing Union-State arrangements and changes in the changed socio-economic context.

q: The Law Commission of India functions primarily as:

options.A: A statutory tribunal for deciding disputes on questions of law
options.B: A constitutional body for the appointment of judges
options.C: An advisory body which undertakes research in law and review of existing laws and recommends legal reforms to the Government
options.D: A department for drafting all Bills to be introduced in Parliament

e: The Law Commission of India is an advisory body that undertakes research in law and review of existing laws and recommends legal reforms to Government; it is neither statutory tribunal nor constitutional body.

q: The Goods and Services Tax was introduced in India through the Constitutional Amendment enacted as the:

options.A: 99th Amendment
options.B: 100th Amendment
options.C: 102nd Amendment
options.D: 101st Amendment

e: GST was introduced through the Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, which inserted Articles 246A, 269A and 279A and amended the Seventh Schedule.

q: Which of the following is excluded from the levy of the Goods and Services Tax?

options.A: Alcoholic liquor for human consumption
options.B: Tobacco products
options.C: Motor vehicles
options.D: Cement

e: Alcoholic liquor for human consumption is excluded from GST under Article 366(12A) and the GST laws; tobacco, motor vehicles and cement remain within GST levy.

q: Under the Goods and Services Tax law, the taxable event, that is, the event on the happening of which the tax becomes leviable, is:

options.A: The manufacture of goods
options.B: The supply of goods or services or both
options.C: The sale of goods only
options.D: The entry of goods into a State

e: Under GST law the taxable event is the supply of goods or services or both, replacing earlier taxable events of manufacture, sale or provision of service.

q: The 'Laffer curve' in public finance illustrates the proposition that:

options.A: Tax revenue rises continuously and proportionately with every increase in the tax rate
options.B: Government expenditure always expands to meet the revenue available
options.C: Beyond an optimum point, an increase in the tax rate may actually reduce the tax revenue, by discouraging work, production and compliance
options.D: The burden of a tax always rests on the person on whom it is first imposed

e: The Laffer curve shows tax revenue first rises with rate but beyond an optimum point a higher rate may reduce revenue by discouraging work, production and compliance.

q: The Coase theorem, relating to externalities, holds in essence that:

options.A: Externalities can be corrected only by a tax equal to the external cost
options.B: Government regulation is always superior to private bargaining
options.C: Property rights have no bearing on the allocation of resources
options.D: Where property rights are clearly defined and transaction costs are low, private bargaining can lead to an efficient outcome regardless of the initial assignment of rights

e: The Coase theorem holds that where property rights are clearly defined and transaction costs are low, private bargaining can reach an efficient outcome regardless of initial assignment of rights.

q: The 'tragedy of the commons' describes the situation in which:

options.A: A resource open to all users, with no effective restriction on access, tends to be overused and depleted because each user seeks to maximise his own gain from it
options.B: Public goods are invariably underpriced by the Government
options.C: Common taxes yield less revenue than separate taxes
options.D: Joint ownership of property between the Centre and the States leads to disputes

e: Tragedy of the commons describes overuse and depletion of a resource open to all with no effective restriction, as each user seeks to maximise his own gain from it.

q: 'Rent seeking' in public economics refers to:

options.A: The fixation of fair rent for Government buildings
options.B: The use of resources to obtain transfers, privileges or artificially created gains through the political and regulatory process, rather than to create new wealth
options.C: The levy of a tax on rental income
options.D: The search for accommodation by Government offices

e: Rent seeking is use of resources to obtain transfers, privileges or artificially created gains through the political and regulatory process, rather than creating new wealth.

q: The 'principal-agent problem' in the working of a public organisation arises principally because:

options.A: The principal is always better informed than the agent
options.B: Public organisations are not subject to any audit
options.C: The persons who carry out the work (agents) may pursue objectives different from those of the authority on whose behalf they act (principal), and the principal cannot observe all their actions fully
options.D: Agents are appointed for a fixed tenure only

e: The principal-agent problem arises because agents may pursue objectives different from the principal and the principal cannot fully observe all agent actions, creating information asymmetry.

q: A 'social audit' of a public programme primarily involves:

options.A: Audit of the programme by a firm of chartered accountants engaged by the implementing agency
options.B: Verification of the programme accounts by the Comptroller and Auditor General alone
options.C: Examination of the social welfare expenditure of the Government as a whole
options.D: Verification of records, works and benefits of the programme by the community and the intended beneficiaries themselves, through public scrutiny

e: Social audit involves verification of records, works and benefits of a programme by the community and intended beneficiaries themselves through public scrutiny and hearings.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes 'reasonable assurance' from 'limited assurance' in an audit or assurance engagement?

options.A: Reasonable assurance is a high level of assurance expressed in a positive form, while limited assurance is a lower level of assurance expressed in a negative form
options.B: Reasonable assurance relates to financial audit, while limited assurance relates only to performance audit
options.C: Limited assurance requires more extensive procedures than reasonable assurance
options.D: There is no difference in the level of assurance conveyed by the two

e: Reasonable assurance is a high level of assurance expressed in positive form, while limited assurance is a lower level expressed in negative form, as in a review engagement.

q: A 'walk-through test' carried out by an auditor consists of:

options.A: A physical inspection of the assets of the audited unit
options.B: Tracing a single transaction from its origin through all the stages of processing and recording in the system, to confirm the auditor's understanding of the process and its controls
options.C: A surprise verification of the cash balance
options.D: A review of the transactions occurring after the close of the year

e: A walk-through test traces a single transaction from origin through all stages of processing and recording to confirm the auditor understanding of the process and its controls.

q: In audit, 'subsequent events' are events which:

options.A: Occurred in a previous financial year but were recorded in the current year
options.B: Are expected to occur in the following financial year
options.C: Occur after the date of the accounts but before the audit report or certificate is issued, and which may require adjustment of, or disclosure in, the accounts
options.D: Occur after the audit report has been laid before the Legislature

e: Subsequent events occur after the date of accounts but before the audit report or certificate is issued, and may require adjustment of, or disclosure in, the accounts.

q: 'Fiscal marksmanship' in budgetary analysis refers to:

options.A: The skill of the Finance Minister in presenting the Budget speech
options.B: The practice of presenting the Budget on the last day of February
options.C: The comparison of revenue deficit with fiscal deficit
options.D: The accuracy of the budgetary forecasts, that is, the closeness with which the Budget Estimates approximate to the actual receipts and expenditure

e: Fiscal marksmanship means accuracy of budgetary forecasts, that is, how closely Budget Estimates approximate to actual receipts and expenditure realised during the year.

q: The Departmentally Related Standing Committees of Parliament examine, among other things:

options.A: Only the Bills referred to them by the Speaker
options.B: Only the reports of the Comptroller and Auditor General
options.C: The Demands for Grants of the Ministries and Departments concerned, after the Budget is presented, and report on them to the Houses
options.D: The nominations for appointment to constitutional posts

e: Departmentally Related Standing Committees examine Demands for Grants of concerned Ministries and Departments after the Budget is presented and report on them to the Houses.

q: The Address of the President to Parliament at the commencement of a session is discussed in the House through:

options.A: An adjournment motion
options.B: A Motion of Thanks moved in the House
options.C: A calling attention notice
options.D: A cut motion on the Demands for Grants

e: The President Address to Parliament is discussed through a Motion of Thanks moved in the House, on which members debate matters referred to in the Address.

q: A 'short duration discussion' in Parliament enables members to:

options.A: Vote on the Demands for Grants without discussion
options.B: Move a motion of no-confidence at short notice
options.C: Raise a discussion on a matter of urgent public importance for a short duration, without a formal motion or voting
options.D: Discuss the Report of the Public Accounts Committee

e: A short duration discussion enables members to raise discussion on a matter of urgent public importance for a short duration, without a formal motion or voting on it.

q: The Committee on Government Assurances of Parliament is concerned with examining:

options.A: The assurances given by the Comptroller and Auditor General to the Public Accounts Committee
options.B: The promises made by candidates at the time of election
options.C: The financial assurances furnished by banks for Government contracts
options.D: The assurances, promises and undertakings given by Ministers on the floor of the House, and the extent to which they have been implemented

e: The Committee on Government Assurances examines assurances, promises and undertakings given by Ministers on the floor of the House and the extent to which they have been implemented.
